Membre de la nation Wet’suwet’en, dont l: A member of the Wet’suwet’en Nation, whose territory is in British Columbia, Marlene Hale has lived in Quebec for a few years. Since last winter, she has been organizing demonstrations in support of her community and speaking out against the GasLink project, which would cross her nation’s territory and has not been approved by the community’s hereditary chiefs. But the pandemic gave her another cause to defend: the mental health of her community during lockdown. In her view, the health crisis is especially hard on Indigenous people. “We’re used to living in community, with family; it’s important to hold on to that,” she says.
Avec son écoute, ses cours de cuisine en: Through her listening, her online cooking classes and traditional Indigenous medicine, Marlene Hale has turned a movement of political mobilization into one of mutual aid and solidarity for Indigenous elders. Zoom has become one of the most popular platforms for remote work, but the cook and activist, with the help of friends, has made it a community space through the webinars Love in the Time of COVID-19: Solidarity and Support for the Elderly. Since the start of lockdown, declared at the end of March, she has gathered dozens of people from across the country every Friday for two hours in her virtual seminars.
« Au début, c’était surtout pour assurer: “At first, it was mostly to maintain political mobilization,” she explains. “It was a way to keep showing our support for the Wet’suwet’en Nation and the Unist’ot’en camp despite the lockdown.” Construction on the Coastal GasLink pipeline, for its part, was not in lockdown and was able to continue through the spring. The purpose of the virtual sessions soon changed. “We realized that elders were the biggest victims of the crisis,” Marlene Hale continues. “So we reoriented the webinars to show them our solidarity. Over the weeks, it became a platform for mental health and for sharing traditional medicine.”
Les webinaires se déroulent en anglais,: The webinars are held in English, but French speakers can take part without worrying about a language barrier. “We have an interpreter, and there’s live translation into French,” Hale says happily. “We’re getting more and more organized.” She also encourages young people in the community to take care of their bodies as much as their minds. A chef by profession, she offers online cooking classes to encourage young Indigenous people to eat well. “I think it’s important to remind people that we have to take care of our whole being, so eating well, going outside, being in nature, moving. That’s how we take care of ourselves,” she says.
« C’est absolument terrible ce qui se pa: “What’s happening is absolutely terrible,” Marlene Hale tells us from her home in Les Cèdres, near Montréal. Recently, five people close to her died by suicide. “It’s a difficult time. Isolation is hard on a lot of people,” she says. “I’m seeing a lot more distress and depression.” The Hope for Wellness Help Line, run by Indigenous Services Canada, has been overwhelmed since the start of the pandemic. Compared with April 2019, the number of calls more than doubled in April of this year. “Counsellors have been added to every shift to handle the increase in call volume,” says a department spokesperson.
Les webinaires de Marlene Hale sont une: Marlene Hale’s webinars give some participants a chance to open up about how they’re feeling. “Everyone is there to give each other advice and support one another. A lot of spirituality and positivity comes out of it,” says Hale. The webinars have led to the creation of a strong community, she notes. And sometimes, they even save lives. “Recently, a young man confided his suicidal thoughts to us and how badly he was doing,” Marlene Hale recounts. “I asked him if he had tobacco to cleanse himself. He said no. So Barbara went to bring him some at his home. He’s doing better.”
« Je lui également donné des graines pou: “I also gave him seeds so he could grow his own and always have some,” adds Barbara Diabo, a Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) from Kahnawake. In many Indigenous communities in North America, tobacco is an important plant used, for example, to cleanse sacred objects and the people taking part in ceremonies. “When you burn tobacco, the smoke can carry our messages to the creator,” Diabo explains. “But it’s okay not to know all the rituals and protocols around it,” she continues. “What matters is the intention behind it, a good and positive intention.”
Les plantes servent à la spiritualité, m: Plants are used for spirituality, but also for health. Marlene Hale’s sister, Charlotte, uses the webinars to teach people how to use plants from Wet’suwet’en territory and make them into, among other things, teas with various properties. “Our mother, Marlene’s and mine, used these teas regularly,” she says. “These days, traditions are so important,” Marlene Hale maintains. “I see how it helps people feel better.” Social intervention worker Jacinthe Connolly, an Ilnu from Mashteuiatsh, has also seen the benefits of traditional rites. “I myself have been shut in for two months,” she says. “I have my rituals every morning with my sage and my pipe.” In her community, she has noticed that lockdown is hard on some people, but “traditional spirituality is for everyone,” she says. “You shouldn’t wait until you’re in distress to practise it; it’s not a magic wand either,” she adds. As the host of the sessions, Marlene Hale welcomes each participant with a smile.
Son tambour traditionnel l’accompagne et: Her traditional drum accompanies her and punctuates the discussions. “Marlene’s warm welcome is so appreciated,” exclaims one participant who lives in Vancouver. Another, of Métis descent, who also lives in Vancouver, echoes that: “I’m very grateful for these moments. It’s wonderful to be able to hear others and share with everyone.”
Les aînés ont toujours une place importa: Elders always have an important place in the webinars. At the start of each session, Barbara Diabo lights a candle that contains tobacco. “It’s to send our prayers for our elders and for those who are taking care of them right now,” she explains. A young non-Indigenous participant is pleased with the place given to elders in Marlene Hale’s webinars. “It’s a beautiful intergenerational space, there’s no age discrimination; it’s one of the things that motivate me to come back every week,” he says. The same participant says he is particularly worried about the situation in long-term care homes in Canada. “Unfortunately, what we’re seeing now is the result of problems that have been building up for years. These facilities are neglected and underfunded,” he laments.
Parallèlement aux webinaires, une campag: Alongside the webinars, a crowdfunding campaign has been set up to help elders. “[The] COVID-19 [crisis] has shown our society’s inability to support elders [...] Through mutual aid, we can overcome our feelings of collective helplessness,” reads the GoFundMe page for the fundraiser.
La majorité des participants proviennent: Most participants are from Canada, “but solidarity is international,” says Marlene Hale. Geoffrey Kamese, from Uganda, is one of the regular participants in the webinars. “He has to stay up until the early morning to be able to talk with us,” Hale says. “It’s great to have a perspective from Africa on the pandemic, and to be able to share how we’re coping with it.”
Kamese rapporte que les mesures de confi: Kamese reports that lockdown and physical distancing measures are hard on many Ugandans. “We too are counting on our solidarity and on our traditional Indigenous medicines,” he says. Kamese’s son recently fell ill, and the virtual seminars were a source of comfort for him. “It makes all the difference to know that we’re supported and that we’re in people’s prayers, even from a distance,” he says.
Marlene Hale souhaite que cette communau: Marlene Hale hopes this community, born online, will continue to exist beyond the COVID-19 pandemic. “We’re there for each other. We’re a family now.”
